title: South Asians in America Have the Highest Heart Risk by Age 45 — Despite Doing Almost Everything Right
excerpt: A landmark study of 2,700 adults found that South Asian Americans report healthier diets, lower alcohol use, and comparable exercise — yet develop diabetes, prediabetes, and hypertension at rates exceeding nearly every other group. Researchers call it a 'paradox' that demands earlier screening.
body:
You eat well. You drink less than your colleagues. You exercise regularly. Your annual physical comes back clean. And yet, by the time you turn 45, you may already be at higher risk for a heart attack than almost anyone else in America.

That is the central and deeply unsettling finding of a landmark longitudinal study from Northwestern Medicine, published in the *Journal of the American Heart Association*. The study — which combined data from the MASALA (Mediators of Atherosclerosis in South Asians Living in America) and MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) cohorts, tracking 2,700 adults over multiple years — found that South Asian Americans develop cardiovascular risk factors earlier and at higher rates than white, Chinese, Black, and Hispanic adults, even while reporting healthier lifestyle behaviours.

## The Numbers That Should Worry You

By age 45, nearly one in three South Asian men in the study had prediabetes. One in four had hypertension. South Asian men also had higher rates of dyslipidemia — abnormal cholesterol and triglyceride levels — than white, Chinese, and Black men.

By age 55, the picture grew starker still: South Asian adults had the highest estimated probability of developing type 2 diabetes among *all* racial and ethnic groups studied. They were at least twice as likely to develop diabetes compared with white adults at the same age.

"The mismatch between healthier lifestyle behaviours and clinical risk was surprising," said senior author Dr. Namratha Kandula, professor of general internal medicine and epidemiology at Northwestern University's Feinberg School of Medicine and a co-founder of the MASALA study. "This paradox tells us we're missing something fundamental to what is driving this elevated risk among South Asians."

## The Lifestyle Paradox



> **""The mismatch between healthier lifestyle behaviours and clinical risk was surprising," said senior author Dr."**


What makes the study so striking is not just the elevated risk — cardiologists have known for decades that South Asians develop heart disease younger — but the paradox that sits beneath it. The South Asian participants in the study reported some of the healthiest behaviours of any group: better diet quality, lower alcohol consumption, and comparable levels of physical activity.

And yet, the clinical markers told a different story. The researchers suggest that standard risk assessment tools, developed primarily on white populations, may systematically underestimate cardiovascular danger in South Asians. Genetic predisposition, metabolic differences including the well-documented "thin-fat" phenotype — in which individuals carry dangerous visceral fat deposits at normal or even low body weights — and potentially epigenetic factors passed across generations may all contribute.

Separate research from McMaster University's START (South Asian Birth Cohort) study has shown that this elevated metabolic risk may begin literally at birth. South Asian newborns, though smaller in stature than white infants, were found to have proportionally more adipose (fat) tissue and higher waist circumference — the "thin-fat" phenotype appearing from day one.


![South Asian Americans — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/94/Top_of_Rock_Cropped.jpg)


"Prevention may be an important way to break the transmission among generations," said Dr. Sonia Anand, the principal investigator and Heart and Stroke Chair in Population Health Research at McMaster.

## A Critical Window in Your Forties

Dr. Kandula emphasised that the study pinpoints a "critical window in the 40s when risk is already high, but disease is still preventable." This has immediate implications for how South Asian Americans — and their doctors — should approach health screening.

The American Heart Association's 2023 scientific statement on South Asian cardiovascular risk recommended several dietary modifications: increasing whole-grain intake, selecting cooking oils lower in saturated fat (a shift from ghee and coconut oil to mustard or olive oil for everyday cooking), and avoiding deep-fried preparation methods. But the Northwestern study suggests that diet alone, even a good one, may not be sufficient.

The researchers argue for earlier, more aggressive screening tailored to South Asian patients. Standard guidelines that recommend cholesterol and blood sugar checks beginning at age 40 or later may be too late for a population in which one-third of men already have prediabetes by 45.

"If you are a South Asian adult, maintain a healthy lifestyle and get screened sooner — check blood pressure, glucose and A1c levels, and cholesterol in early adulthood rather than waiting for symptoms," Dr. Kandula advised.

## What the Diaspora Needs to Hear

For the roughly 5.4 million South Asian Americans — and millions more across the UK, Canada, and Australia — this study carries an urgent message: doing the right things is necessary but may not be enough. The biological deck is stacked in ways that conventional medicine is only beginning to understand, and the standard one-size-fits-all approach to cardiovascular screening was not designed with South Asian bodies in mind.

The practical takeaways are clear. First, get screened earlier — ideally in your late 30s rather than waiting for your 40s. Push for a comprehensive metabolic panel that includes fasting glucose, HbA1c, a full lipid panel, and a waist-to-hip ratio measurement (which captures visceral fat more accurately than BMI). Second, be aware that a "normal" BMI does not guarantee metabolic health in South Asians — the traditional BMI cutoffs of 25 for overweight and 30 for obese significantly underestimate risk in this population. Third, share this information with ageing parents, many of whom receive infrequent or culturally misaligned healthcare both in the diaspora and back in India.

The MASALA study, now in its second decade, remains one of the only large-scale longitudinal studies specifically designed to understand cardiovascular risk in South Asian Americans. Its findings have already informed AHA guidelines. But its most important contribution may be the simplest: telling an entire community that the rules of the game are different for them — and that knowing that early enough could be the difference between prevention and crisis.

---

*Sources: Journal of the American Heart Association (MASALA/MESA longitudinal analysis, Northwestern Medicine); American Heart Association Scientific Statement on South Asian ASCVD Risk (2023); McMaster University START Birth Cohort Study; Northwestern University press release.*
